newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour promises rail watchdog with bite.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour promises rail watchdog with bite.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party on Wednesday promised a regulatory clampdown on the rail industry if it wins the next election, citing franchise operators and Railtrack Plc as the most likely targets.
Labour transport spokesman Andrew Smith also promised speedy action to tackle the London Underground railway's funding crisis.
But he said Labour would stick to the existing budget for the system, adding that he would publish more details on plans for the "tube" in the coming weeks.
Labour is tipped to win the next election, widely expected to be held on May 1, as it rides high in the opinion polls against the ruling Conservative Party.

In an interview with Reuters, Smith said he saw transport as a key election issue. "I think it is a vote winner. People see chaos, mounting congestion and a fragmented transport network as a consequence of Tory neglect."

The existing regulatory regime for governing the newly privatised rail industry, in particular, was inadequate, he said. The issue of investment by Railtrack, which owns the rail network infrastructure, was a big concern.

"There is already a 700 million (pound) backlog. Railtrack is a national monopoly and its investment is critical nationwide. We certainly won't be deflected by any delaying tactics which may be used by Railtrack," he said.

Smith said the maximum powers available were not being used to govern Railtrack, which was privatised last May. "But the regulator can initiate a change to Railtrack's licence and can also seek to amend its track access conditions," he said.
Smith was referring to Railtrack's price review due in 2001 which could be made tougher for Railtrack if it failed to comply with its obligations.
Britain's 25 passenger franchises also pay Railtrack for use of its infrastructure. Smith said track access conditions could be changed to reflect Railtrack's failure to meet investment obligations.
A third option is understood to be legislation setting a target or minimum investment requirement for Railtrack.

The train operating companies (TOCs) privatised from the former British Rail also face a tougher regime if Labour wins. Smith said that South West Trains' controversial cancellation of many of its train services in recent weeks as a result of a shortage of drivers was evidence that regulation was not tough enough.
"The penalty regime is not being used to the full. One of the proofs is the South West Trains affair," he said. South West Trains is owned by Stagecoach Holdings Plc.
Labour wants publication of performance against franchise commitments and disclosure of fines.
Smith envisages the creation of one transport regulator governing rail and buses. But buses will have a looser regulatory system than rail.
On the tube plans, Smith said: "We're in consultation with financial experts and London Transport over options and we are confident we will be able to move quickly once elected."

Labour would "adhere to the existing budget constraints", he said, appearing to rule out any emergency cash injection into the network. Smith said he had held "positive and helpful" talks with London Transport, the nationalised body reponsible for the tube.

Labour has ruled out privatisation of the underground, a policy which the Conservative government is committed to if it wins the election. The government says the sale could raise up to two billion pounds ($3.2 billion). ($ = 0.629 British Pounds)
